findings.label: 16-bit large shapes saturate the AIV instruction stream; memory pipes idle
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof PipeUtilization ratios per AIV core; 40 AIV units inferred from aiv_total_cycles / (kernel_time x 1.65 GHz).

evidence.value: MTE2 bandwidth utilization lower than 80% when active; MTE3 bandwidth utilization lower than 80% when active

evidence.metric: block dim (grid) confirmed for the 512-program geometry

findings.inference: aiv_vec_ratio + aiv_scalar_ratio is 0.955 (float16::3), 0.944 (bfloat16::3) and 1.010 (float16::0), i.e. the AIV instruction stream is essentially fully occupied, while MTE2/MTE3 are at most 0.445/0.178. These four workloads are therefore issue-limited on the vector core, not memory-limited; the msprof report independently states MTE2/MTE3 utilisation stays below 80% when active. For a kernel at ~0.95-1.01 issue occupancy, no launch geometry or DMA-pipeline change can recover more than a few percent - only fewer vector instructions per element can.

findings.label: Second pipeline stage on the 1G 16-bit loop had no headroom (frozen-plan sub-hypothesis contradicted)
findings.backend_detail: num_stages=2 keeps the runtime loop DMA-resident but the loop is compute-bound at this size.
findings.inference: With the vector issue stream at 1.01 and the load pipe under half busy, a second software-pipeline stage has no latency to hide. This explains the trusted eval comparison for the 1G class: float16::0 went 7.5389 -> 7.5538 ms (-0.2%) and bfloat16::4 7.8038 -> 7.8126 ms (-0.1%) after LOOP_STAGES_BIG=2 was introduced, i.e. the predicted +1.9% did not transfer from the target-side sweep. By contrast the 512-program/8192-tile part of the plan is supported: float16::2 -4.6%, float16::3 -4.0%, bfloat16::2 -2.4%, bfloat16::3 -1.9% in the same comparison.

findings.label: fp32 large shapes run at the achieved memory roofline (~1.17-1.19 TB/s aggregate)
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof MTE2 (GM->UB) and MTE3 (UB->GM) duty per AIV.

evidence.metric: derived aggregate traffic rate (12.883 GB moved in 10.8466 ms)
derived aggregate traffic rate (201.3 MB moved in 172.872 us)

findings.inference: Both fp32 large shapes move 12 bytes per element and both land at 1164-1187 GB/s aggregate, with the vector pipe at 0.571-0.576 and the two DMA pipes together at 0.90-1.09 duty; per-element kernel time is 10.1 ps (1G) and 10.3 ps (16.7M), i.e. essentially bytes/bandwidth. The fp32 path is therefore byte-limited at the memory system's measured throughput ceiling, so a deeper pipeline or a different program/tile geometry has at most single-digit-percent headroom - and the 16.7M fp32 case, whose working set (201 MB) already exceeds the 176 MB L2, shows the same ceiling with the memory pipes only 0.90 busy. Note the contrast with the 16-bit cases: 6 bytes/element at this bandwidth would be 5.1 ps/element, but they take 6.95-7.08 ps/element, i.e. 26-28% above the roofline time.

findings.label: Per-element vector cost is dtype-independent, so 16-bit paths pay the fp32-domain element function plus conversions
findings.backend_detail: Triton/Ascend lowers the shared element function identically for all three dtypes; only the conversion instructions differ.

evidence.metric: aiv_mte2_ratio with a fully L2-resident working set (100.7 MB < 176 MB L2)

findings.inference: The fp32-domain vector work per element is 5.77-6.56 ps for fp32, fp16 and bfloat16 alike, even though the input width differs by 2x; this matches the source, where the correction is always evaluated in fp32 and the 16-bit paths add fp16/bfloat16<->fp32 conversions. Since float16::3 is memory-free (mte2 0.205 with an L2-resident working set) yet takes 6.95 ps/element, its deficit against the native reference (5.71 ps/element) is per-element compute efficiency, not memory. This is the only remaining lever for the four sub-1.0-speedup workload classes, and it must come from fewer fp32 vector instructions in _lad2_elem.

findings.label: Smallest shape is scalar/dispatch-bound, not vector-bound
findings.inference: For the 4096-element shape only 56% of the measured op duration is AIV work, and within that work scalar issue (0.439) exceeds vector issue (0.319). These workloads already win (1.30-1.39x) and are dominated by per-launch setup/dispatch, so instruction-count reductions cannot help them; msprof also warns its timing is diagnostic and not the eval latency (eval 1.466 us vs 1.763 us here).

performance_interpretation: Round 6 added +0.96% geo_mean (1.2552 -> 1.2673) and the profile explains both halves of that plan. The 512-program, 8192-tile runtime loop for 16.7M 16-bit inputs is real progress: it is confirmed at Block Dim 512 and the eval shows -4.6%/-4.0% latency on float16::2/::3 and -2.4%/-1.9% on bfloat16::2/::3. The second half of the plan - LOOP_STAGES_BIG=2 for the 1G loop - is not supported by the hardware evidence: the 1G 16-bit loop runs with aiv_vec_ratio 0.9266 plus aiv_scalar_ratio 0.0835, i.e. the vector issue stream is already 101% occupied, so a deeper DMA stage has nothing to hide, and the eval shows float16::0 and bfloat16::4 flat to -0.2%. The kernel now splits cleanly into three regimes. (1) 16-bit large shapes (all four sub-1.0-speedup fp16 workloads and the bfloat16 winners) are AIV-issue-bound at 0.94-1.01 vector+scalar occupancy with 40-75% memory slack; geometry work there is exhausted and the residual 21% gap to the native fp16 reference is per-element compute, since the shared element function always evaluates the correction in fp32 (~6.1-6.3 ps of vector time per element versus 5.77 ps for the pure-fp32 path, which has no conversion instructions). (2) fp32 large shapes are byte-limited at 1164-1187 GB/s aggregate with the memory pipes 0.90-1.09 busy and only 0.57 vector occupancy; at 12 bytes per element there is little left to take. (3) Small shapes are setup/dispatch-bound and already above 1.3x. The highest-value remaining action is therefore to remove fp32 vector instructions from the element function used by the 16-bit paths, betting that the 0.95-1.01 issue occupancy converts instruction savings into time almost linearly.

next_experiment.action_description: Shorten the fp32-domain instruction stream in the shared element function _lad2_elem for the 16-bit paths while keeping the correction in fp32: replace the current 't = tl.abs(xf - yf)' followed by the two-instruction clamp 'tl.where(t <= 200.0, t, 200.0)' with the single saturating clamp 't = tl.minimum(tl.abs(xf - yf), 200.0)'. This removes one fp32 compare plus select (the equivalent of ~1 of roughly 16-20 fp32 vector instructions per element) from a kernel whose AIV issue stream is already 0.94-1.01 occupied. Leave the operand-dtype maximum, the natural-log form of the correction and the single final rounding exactly as they are, and leave the launch geometry untouched so the round-6 gains cannot be disturbed.
next_experiment.expected_impact: 4-6% lower kernel latency on the nine vector-issue-bound 16-bit large workloads: float16::0/::2/::3/::4 from 0.824-0.949 toward roughly 0.86-0.99, bfloat16::0/::2/::3/::4 from 1.56-1.59 toward roughly 1.63-1.66, i.e. headline geo_mean from 1.267 toward about 1.29-1.31. The memory-bound fp32 large shapes are expected to be unchanged.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: The only numerical risk is NaN handling: tl.minimum may propagate a NaN |x-y| instead of saturating it, in which case the equal-infinity case would yield NaN instead of inf and test_logaddexp2_non_finite[dtype0..2] would fail. Validate that workload first. If it fails, restore the tl.where clamp (identical op budget) or move the clamp onto the exponent argument, and re-run; the 5-D ragged and broadcast correctness workloads must also be re-checked because _lad2_elem is shared by every launch path. Rollback is a one-expression revert in _lad2_elem with no geometry, launch or numerics change elsewhere, so the round-6 improvements are preserved either way.

open_questions: Would re-running instruction-level profiling on a smaller 16-bit workload (for example float16::2 at 1M elements instead of 16.7M) fit the simulator deadline and reveal the instruction mix, allowing the next step to target the dominant instruction class rather than the cheapest one?

The two DMA pipes are 0.90 busy at 16.7M fp32 but 1.09 at 1G fp32 with essentially the same achieved aggregate bandwidth; is the 1G case losing a few percent to read/write interleaving, or is 1.17-1.19 TB/s simply this part's ceiling?

Is the 2.4% higher vector time of bfloat16::3 versus float16::3 (105.2 us versus 102.7 us at identical shape and element size) due to a more expensive bfloat16 conversion sequence, and would it be worth using the same log/exp formulation but a different conversion path?
Removing the num_stages=2 setting for the 1G 16-bit loop is behaviourally neutral per the evidence; should it be reverted to reduce compile complexity, given it measured flat to -0.2% in eval?
